Valve timing in one cardiac cycle
The mitral and tricuspid valves open to fill the ventricles; both outflow valves stay shut.
All four valves are closed while pressure rises in the ventricles without a change in volume.
The aortic and pulmonary valves open for ejection; both inlet valves stay shut.
The outflow valves close. All four are shut briefly while the ventricles relax at fixed volume.
Aorta
The main systemic artery carries blood from the left ventricle to its branches. Its elastic wall helps sustain arterial flow between beats.
aortic arch ascending aorta
Aortic ejection and recoil
Left ventricular pressure rises above aortic pressure.
The aortic valve opens and the proximal aorta expands during ejection.
The aortic valve closes as the ventricular pressure falls.
Elastic recoil helps drive blood onward into systemic branches.
Pulmonary trunk
The first segment of the pulmonary arterial pathway carries blood from the right ventricle and divides into the left and right pulmonary arteries.
pulmonary outflow main pulmonary artery
Blood flow through the pulmonary trunk
Right ventricular pressure rises during contraction.
The pulmonary valve opens when the ventricular pressure exceeds pressure in the trunk.
Flow divides into the pulmonary arteries toward both lungs.
The pulmonary valve closes as right ventricular pressure falls.
Right atrium
Receives systemic venous return and blood from the coronary sinus, then supplies the right ventricle through the tricuspid valve.
RA right atrial chamber
Right atrial filling and emptying
Blood returns from the venae cavae and coronary sinus.
When the tricuspid valve opens, blood passes into the relaxed right ventricle.
Atrial contraction adds to the final filling of the right ventricle.
The tricuspid valve closes with ventricular contraction; the atrium receives more venous blood.
Left atrium
Receives blood from the pulmonary veins and moves it through the mitral valve into the left ventricle.
LA left atrial chamber
Left atrial transfer to the ventricle
Pulmonary venous blood accumulates in the atrium.
The mitral valve opens when atrial pressure exceeds left ventricular pressure.
Left atrial contraction completes ventricular filling.
Mitral closure isolates the atrium from the contracting left ventricle.
Right ventricle
Pumps blood through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk. Its wall is thinner than the wall of the left ventricle.
RV right ventricular chamber
Right ventricular pumping
The chamber fills from the right atrium through the tricuspid valve.
The tricuspid valve closes and the right ventricle builds pressure before ejection.
The pulmonary valve opens and blood enters the pulmonary trunk.
The ventricle relaxes and the pulmonary valve closes, limiting backflow.
Left ventricle
Its thick muscular wall generates the pressure that sends blood through the aortic valve into the systemic circulation.
LV left ventricular chamber
Left ventricular pumping
Blood enters from the left atrium through the open mitral valve.
The mitral valve closes; left ventricular pressure rises without ejection.
The aortic valve opens and left ventricular volume falls as blood enters the aorta.
The aortic valve closes while the left ventricle relaxes.
Tricuspid valve
The right atrioventricular valve controls flow from the right atrium to the right ventricle. Chordae and papillary muscles help stop the leaflets from inverting during contraction.
right AV valve
Tricuspid opening and closure
During filling the open tricuspid valve lets blood enter the right ventricle.
As right ventricular pressure rises, the tricuspid leaflets close.
The valve remains shut during ejection into the pulmonary trunk.
It remains closed during early relaxation until right ventricular pressure drops below atrial pressure.
Mitral valve
The left atrioventricular valve allows blood from the left atrium into the left ventricle. Its two leaflets are supported by chordae and papillary muscles.
bicuspid valve left AV valve
Mitral opening and closure
The open mitral valve allows left ventricular filling.
When left ventricular pressure exceeds left atrial pressure, the leaflets meet.
The valve stays shut while the left ventricle ejects blood to the aorta.
It does not reopen until relaxing ventricular pressure falls below that of the left atrium.
Pulmonary valve
The semilunar valve between the right ventricle and pulmonary trunk limits return of blood into the ventricle after ejection.
pulmonary semilunar valve
Pulmonary valve ejection timing
The valve is closed while the right ventricle fills.
It remains shut as early contraction raises right ventricular pressure.
It opens when the right ventricle can push blood into the pulmonary trunk.
As right ventricular pressure falls below trunk pressure, the cusps close.
Aortic valve
The semilunar valve at the left ventricular outlet prevents blood in the aorta from returning to the ventricle after ejection.
aortic semilunar valve
Aortic valve ejection timing
The higher pressure on the aortic side holds the valve shut during filling.
Early ventricular contraction does not yet open the valve.
The cusps open when left ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure.
Falling ventricular pressure allows a brief reverse flow that closes the cusps.
